newsitem.title: FRANCE: Salinger claims "proof" on TWA missile theory.
newsitem.headline: Salinger claims "proof" on TWA missile theory.

text.p: Former U.S. presidential spokesman Pierre Salinger waded back into the controversy over last year's crash of a TWA jumbo jet on Thursday, presenting what he called proof it was shot down by a U.S. Navy missile.

The evidence, dismissed in advance by U.S. investigators, consisted mostly of radar images Salinger said backed a theory that the U.S. Navy accidentally shot down Trans World Airlines flight 800 off New York on July 17, killing all 230 aboard.

Salinger and a journalistic team headed by Dr Mike Sommers, an investigative reporter, compiled their allegations in a 69-page report he said proved their case. The images were published simultaneously in the French magazine Paris Match.
Salinger alleged that the Navy, U.S. military intelligence and the FBI have been engaged in a vast cover-up to hide their responsibility for the disaster.

"That (radar) tape done by the air traffic control completely confirms that a missile fired down TWA 800," Salinger told a news conference. "We have now reached the point where we are totally sure that what we are saying is true."
Salinger, who was spokesman for president John F. Kennedy, called for a full investigation into his allegations by U.S. Secretary of Defence William Cohen.
U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Chairman Jim Hall, echoing comments from the FBI on Wednesday, rejected Salinger's theory.
"Right now we have no evidence, no physical evidence that a missile or bomb exploded and caused that accident," he said on the NBC "Today Show". He added: "We have not seen any missile track."

"I think what Mr. Salinger is saying is that the Navy shot the plane down. I think the FBI have looked at that. I think that's wrong...It's just irresponsible even to allege that the men and women in our service, if something like that happened, that there would be some kind of coverup."

"If at any time we have any evidence of criminal activity we will make that known to the FBI," Hall said. Salinger said at the news conference that he had given his team's report to the FBI four days ago.

French foreign ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told a news briefing Paris understood the impatience of families of victims, many of whom were French, but had "full confidence in the results which will emerge from the U.S. investigation".

Sommers said the images from a radar videotape from John F. Kennedy airport showed an unidentified plane, which he said was a U.S. Navy Orion P3 surveillance aircraft, and another blip that he said showed a missile racing toward the airliner.

Sommers also showed photographs which he said pictured a U.S. Navy Tomahawk cruise missile in the air near where the plane crashed. The photographs were first uncovered last year and dismissed by U.S. government investigators.
Salinger's theories, including a previous set excluded by investigators last year, touch a nerve because the cause of the Paris-bound crash on July 17 is still a mystery.
NTSB and FBI investigators have indicated that mechanical failure rather than a bomb or missile may have been responsible for the explosion on the Paris-bound flight.
Salinger said he believed the U.S. Navy fired a missile from the sea, perhaps from a submarine, and that electronic equipment aboard the TWA plane lured the missile off course to hit it.

Salinger and his team were paid an undisclosed sum for the Paris Match article. Sommers told reporters the money would go to families of TWA flight 800 victims but Salinger said he needed his share to cover expenses.
